## Loading in data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
pubmed <- read_csv("~/Downloads/pubmed.csv")
pubmed
```

# Text Mining

## Question 1

```{r}
library(tidytext)
library(dplyr)
pubmed |> group_by(term) |> count(term, name="# of abstracts")

token_counts <- pubmed |>
  unnest_tokens(token, abstract) |> group_by(term) |>
  count(token, sort = TRUE) 
token_counts

top_five_tokens <- token_counts |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(n)) |>
  ungroup()
top_five_tokens

```

There are 981 abstacts for the term covid, 376 abstracts for the term cystic fibrosis, 317 abstracts for the term meningitis, 780 abstracts for the term preeclampsia, and 787 abstracts for the term prostrate cancer.

After tokenizing the abstracts and counting the number of each token from highest to lowest, I did not find any token terms that were interesting in the first 10 displayed rows for terms of covid, preeclampsia, and prostate cancer. Most of the terms seem to be filler words in a sentence and don't have a meaningful explanation to what the abstract will be about. When I look at the last 10 rows, I find that these tokens appear less often but seem to be more informative to what the abstract will be about especially for terms of covid, meningitis, preeclampsia, and prostrate cancer.

The 5 most common tokens for the search term covid include "the, of, covid, 19, and". For the search term cystic fibrosis and preeclampsia, the most common 5 tokens include "the, of, and, in, to." The 5 most common tokens in the search term meningitis include "the, of, and, in, a." For prostate cancer, the 5 most common tokens are "the, of, and, prostrate, cancer."

## Question 2

```{r}
stop_words |>
  filter(lexicon == "snowball") |>
  pull(word)

pubmed_stop <- pubmed |>
  unnest_tokens(token, abstract) |>
   group_by(term) |>
  anti_join(stop_words, by = c("token" = "word")) |>
  count(token, sort = TRUE)
pubmed_stop

top_five_tokens_stop <- pubmed_stop |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  arrange(term, desc(n)) |>
  ungroup()
top_five_tokens_stop
```

After removing stop words from the pubmed dataset, the top 10 most tokens that appear across all the search terms are "covid, 19, cancer, prostate,patients, pre, eclampsia, preeclampsia, women, and pregnancy." Without stop words, the top 10 most tokens that appeared were "the, of, covid, the, 19, and, of, the, of, and."

The top 5 tokens for the search term covid after removing the stop words are "covid, 19, patients, disease, pandemic." For cystic fibrosis, the top 5 tokens are "fibrosis, cystic, cf, patients, disease" after removing stop words. The top 5 tokens of th term meningitis after removing stop words are "patients, meningitis, meningeal, csf, clinical." Preeclampsia had the top 5 tokens after removing stop words, which include "pre, eclampsia, preeclampsia, women, pregnancy." The term prostrate cancer had the top 5 most tokens as "cancer, prostate, patients, treatment, disease" after removing stop words.

## Question 3

```{r}
pubmed |>
  unnest_tokens(
    ngram,
    abstract,
    token = "ngrams",
    n = 2
  ) |>
  count(ngram, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(ngram, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Count",
    y = "Bigram",
    title = "10 Most Common Bigrams in PubMed Abstracts"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
    
```

## Question 4

```{r}
pubmed |>
  unnest_tokens(token, abstract) |>
  count(token, term) |>
  bind_tf_idf(token, term, n) |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = tf_idf,
    n = 5,
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  arrange(term, desc(tf_idf)) |>
  ungroup()
```

For covid search term, the 5 tokens with the highest TF-IDF values are "covid, pandemic, coronavirus, sars, cov" and for cystic fibrosis, the 5 tokens with the highest TF-IDF are "cf, fibrosis, cystic, cftr, sweat." Meningitis has the top 5 TF-IDF values for tokens: "meningitis, meningeal, pachymeningitis, csf, meninges." Preeclampsia has the top 5 TF-IDF values for tokens: "eclampsia, preeclampsia, pregnancy, maternal, gestational." For prostate cancer search term, the 5 tokens with the highest TF-IDF value are "prostate, androgen, psa, prostatectomy, castration."

Compared to question 1, these top 5 TF-IDF value tokens are more informative than the top 5 tokens that appeared across all the search terms in question 1 because those tokens were filler words. Covid did appear as a token in the search term covid for this question and question 1. Similarly, prostate also appeared as a frequent token in this exercise and in question 1. These differences are attributed to the TF-IDF value since TF measures how frequently a word appears in a single search term or "document," and IDF measures how rare or common this word appears across all abstracts. A high TF-IDF score indicates that the word does appear frequently in that single abstract but rarely across the rest of the collection of abstracts, making it a signature keyword. This occurs because as we see in Question 1, most common words like "the", "is", or "and" appear often among many abstracts and are heavily downweighted while unique words are given more weight. Therefore, this exercises pulls out the top 5 words that don't appear as often and more meaningful to the search term than filler words that are extremely common.

# Sentiment Analysis

```{r}
library(textdata)
get_sentiments('nrc')
get_sentiments('afinn')
```

## Question 5

```{r}
pubmed_nrc <- pubmed |>
  unnest_tokens(token, abstract) |>
  inner_join(
    get_sentiments("nrc"),
    by = c("token" = "word"),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )

most_common_sentiment <- pubmed_nrc |>
    count(term, sentiment) |>
    group_by(term) |>
    slice_max(order_by = n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) 
most_common_sentiment

sentiment_removed <- pubmed_nrc |>
  filter(!sentiment %in% c("positive", "negative")) |>
  count(term, sentiment) |>
  group_by(term) |>
  slice_max(order_by = n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
sentiment_removed
```

Using the NRC lexicon, the most common sentiment for each search term is "positive" or "negative." The most common sentiment for the search terms covid, cystic fibrosis, preeclampsia is "positive" and the most common sentiment for the search terms meningitis and prostrate cancer is "negative." If I remove "positive" or "negative" from the NRC list, "fear" shows up as the most common sentiment in the search terms covid, meningitis, and prostate cancer. After removal of the "positive" and "negative" sentiment from the NRC lexicon list, "disgust" is the most common sentiment for the search term cystic fibrosis and "anticipation" is the most common sentiment for the search term preeclampsia.

## Question 6

```{r}
pubmed_afinn <- pubmed |>
  mutate(abstract_id = row_number()) |>
  unnest_tokens(token, abstract) |>
  inner_join(
    get_sentiments("afinn"),
    by = c("token" = "word")
  ) |>
  group_by(abstract_id, term) |>
  summarise(sentiment = mean(value),
            .groups="drop")

pubmed_afinn
```

The average positivity score for each abstract could be negative, indicating more negative language, or they could be positive, indicating more positive language.

```{r}
ggplot(pubmed_afinn, aes(x = term, y = sentiment)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Positivity Score by Search Term",
    x = "Search term",
    y = "Average AFINN score per abstract"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

According to the plot, cystic fibrosis has a higher and positive median of abstracts' average positivity scores compared to other search terms, which demonstrates more positive language. The other search terms have lower medians of the average positivity scores and are negative medians, indicating more negative language. Prostate cancer shows less variability in the abstracts' average positivity scores whereas cystic fibrosis has greater variability. The distributions of all the search terms overlap, which means that the abstracts from all the search terms have similar average positivity scores.
